title: The Life Behind the Screen
content:
By the time Lucas realized that his life had become something he was constantly documenting, he had already forgotten what it felt like to experience a moment without thinking about how it would look on a screen.

His mornings began with notifications.

Before getting out of bed, he checked messages, responded to comments, and opened the applications that had gradually become part of his routine. He knew which photographs performed well, which subjects generated discussion, and which times of day produced the greatest engagement.

He also knew something else.

He was tired.

One Saturday morning, his sister, Clara, arrived unexpectedly at his apartment.

— You look exhausted.

Lucas put his phone on the table.

— I didn't sleep well.

— You were online until two in the morning.

He looked at her.

— How do you know?

— Because you posted at 1:47.

Lucas laughed.

— You're keeping track?

— Apparently, I don't have to. You keep telling everyone.

She sat down beside him.

— When was the last time you went somewhere without taking a picture?

Lucas thought about it.

He couldn't remember.

— I don't know.

— That's the problem.

He picked up his phone again.

— It's my job.

— Is it?

He frowned.

— What do you mean?

— I mean, if you hadn't turned your hobby into a job, would you still enjoy it?

The question stayed with him long after Clara had left.

That evening, Lucas attended a friend's birthday dinner.

There were twelve people around the table, but almost everyone had a phone within reach.

When the food arrived, three people immediately took photographs.

Someone asked everyone to wait before eating.

— We need a picture first.

Lucas instinctively reached for his phone.

Then he stopped.

He looked around the table.

Nobody was talking.

Everyone was arranging the food, adjusting the lighting, checking the screen.

He put his phone away.

— What's wrong? — his friend asked.

— Nothing.

— Aren't you taking a picture?

Lucas smiled.

— No.

His friend laughed.

— That's unusual.

— I know.

For the first time in months, Lucas ate dinner without photographing it.

He listened to conversations.

He laughed at stories that would never appear online.

He noticed the sound of rain against the windows.

When he returned home, he realized that he could remember the evening more clearly than he could remember most of the photographs he had taken during the previous year.

The following Monday, Lucas received an offer from a large company.

They wanted him to create a series of daily videos documenting his lifestyle.

The contract was generous.

The conditions were demanding.

He would have to publish every day.

He would have to make his personal routines part of the campaign.

He would have to allow the company to use his image for two years.

Lucas read the contract twice.

Then he called Clara.

— I have an offer.

— Is it good?

— Financially? Very.

— And otherwise?

He hesitated.

— I'm not sure.

— Then don't answer yet.

— Why?

— Because you're always asking whether something will perform well. Ask yourself whether you'll still want it when nobody is watching.

Lucas looked at the contract.

If he accepted, his audience would probably grow considerably.

His income would increase.

His career could change completely.

But he also knew that he would be giving up even more privacy.

— What would you do? — he asked.

— I wouldn't make the decision for you.

— That's not helpful.

— It is. You just don't like it.

She paused.

— You need to decide what kind of life you want before deciding what kind of content you want to create.

Lucas spent the next few days thinking about his relationship with social media.

He remembered when he had first started posting photographs.

There had been no strategy.

No analytics.

No sponsorships.

He had simply enjoyed sharing things that interested him.

Somewhere along the way, he had begun measuring everything.

Views.

Likes.

Comments.

Followers.

Engagement.

He had stopped asking whether something was meaningful and started asking whether it was clickable.

On Friday morning, he made a decision.

He turned down the contract.

Then he posted a short message explaining why.

He expected criticism.

There was plenty.

Some followers accused him of being ungrateful.

Others said he was wasting an opportunity.

A few people unfollowed him.

But something unexpected happened.

Thousands of people responded by describing their own struggles with constantly comparing themselves to others online.

One message particularly caught his attention.

I thought I was the only person who felt like my life wasn't real unless I posted it. Thank you for saying this.

Lucas read it several times.

Then he closed the application.

Months later, Lucas still used social media.

He hadn't abandoned it.

Instead, he had changed the way he used it.

He no longer posted every day.

He sometimes disappeared for an entire weekend.

When he traveled, he occasionally waited until he returned before sharing photographs.

When he met friends, he tried to remain present instead of documenting every conversation.

His audience became smaller.

But more engaged.

And, more importantly, he became happier.

One afternoon, Clara found him sitting in a park without his phone.

She smiled.

— I thought you'd lost it.

— I left it at home.

— On purpose?

— On purpose.

She sat beside him.

— How does it feel?

Lucas looked at the people walking around them.

Children were playing. Someone was reading beneath a tree. Two elderly men were arguing over a chessboard.

None of them were recording anything.

— Strange.

— Good strange or bad strange?

He smiled.

— Good.

Clara nodded.

— Do you miss having thousands of people watching everything you do?

Lucas thought for a moment.

— Sometimes.

— And then?

— Then I remember that they weren't really watching me.

She looked at him.

— What do you mean?

— They were watching what I chose to show them.

He leaned back against the bench.

— I spent years trying to create a perfect version of my life. Eventually, I couldn't tell whether I was living my life or managing its image.

Clara smiled.

— And now?

Lucas looked toward the sky.

— Now I'm trying to live first and post later.

She laughed.

— That sounds almost revolutionary.

— In 2026, maybe it is.

They sat quietly for a while.

Lucas knew that social media was not disappearing.

Neither was the pressure to share, compare, react, and perform.

Technology would continue changing the way people communicated. New platforms would appear, old ones would disappear, and new forms of digital identity would emerge.

But Lucas had learned something that no algorithm could measure.

A moment did not become more valuable because thousands of people had seen it.

A life did not become more meaningful because it had been carefully presented.

And happiness did not require an audience.

He had spent years believing that if he could make his life look perfect, he would eventually feel perfect too.

He had been wrong.

The screen had never been the problem.

Forgetting to look beyond it had been.
